The newly hatched larva, emerging from a gelatinous egg mass after an incubation period of 10 days [ab = 10 days] at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C], weighs a mere 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], reflecting the small initial yolk reserves typically found in anurans with multiple clutch cycles. This initial mass scales up considerably during the free-swimming tadpole phase, which transitions to a post-metamorphic juvenile at a size of 1.63 centimeters  following metamorphosis. The timing of this transformation from a gill-breathing larva into a terrestrial toadlet occurs after approximately 106 days after hatching  under controlled thermal conditions of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a value that falls near the median of the 86- to 125-day range reported elsewhere for the species.

The energetic implications of such dimorphism are substantial, given that a gravid female must support both her own somatic demands and the production of several thousand eggs per clutch.

Although no formal clutch-frequency data exist for wild populations, the species is thought to deposit eggs in multiple small batches rather than a single large mass, a bet-hedging strategy that mitigates the risk of desiccation in ephemeral breeding pools typical of Ladakh's arid montane zone.

Comparing the demographic parameters of Bufotes viridis with those of other Bufotes species reveals a suite of adaptations to cold, arid environments. The juvenile period, lasting about 106 days from hatching  to metamorphosis at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], is relatively extended compared to that of lowland bufonids, likely reflecting cooler water temperatures in high-elevation breeding ponds, which slow larval development.
